title: OUCH 5.0
text: Market data shows you the book. Order entry is how you change it. On Nasdaq, the native way in is OUCH: a small, binary, fixed-layout protocol.

title: Two pipes
text: A trading firm holds two connections to the exchange. ITCH flows one way, and tells everyone what happened. OUCH flows both ways, and only you see it. Your orders go up inside SoupBinTCP unsequenced packets. The exchange's answers come back as sequenced packets, so after a reconnect you can replay every one you missed.

title: Enter Order · 47 bytes
text: A new order is message type O, and it is 47 bytes long. First a four byte UserRefNum, your number for this order. Then the side, and a four byte quantity. An eight byte symbol, and an eight byte price. Five one-byte flags: time in force, display, capacity, intermarket sweep, and cross type. A fourteen byte ClOrdID, free text for your own records. And a two byte appendage length, for optional fields that follow.

title: A worked example
text: Say we buy 100 shares at 187 dollars 25. Prices carry four implied decimals, so the wire holds the integer 1,872,500, big-endian. The symbol is left-justified and padded with spaces. Time in force zero means a day order. The exchange answers with Order Accepted, 64 bytes, echoing our fields plus its own order reference number. When someone trades with us, Order Executed arrives: 36 bytes, with shares, price, a liquidity flag, and a match number.

title: UserRefNum
text: UserRefNum is the key to the whole protocol. It must be unique and strictly increasing, per account, for the whole day. A lower number is not an error: the exchange ignores it as a retransmission. So resending after a reconnect can never create a duplicate order. And if you lose count, Account Query returns the next number the exchange expects.

title: In the lab
text: In the lab, libs slash ouch describes each message once, as a list of offsets and fields. That one list drives both encode and decode. A compile-time check fails the build if the list does not end at the spec's length. The trader's order entry thread owns the socket, so the trading thread never makes a system call. And simex checks the UserRefNum, quantity and price before an order reaches the matching engine.

title: Pitfalls
text: Three details catch newcomers. Prices are integers: the highest limit is 199,999 dollars 99, and 214,748.3647 marks a market order. Every integer is big-endian. And every message ends with an appendage length, even when it is zero. Get those right, and OUCH is the shortest path from a decision to the book.
